newsitem.title: UK: Use drugs only for very obese, British doctors say.
newsitem.headline: Use drugs only for very obese, British doctors say.

text.p: Slimming drugs should be used only for the clinically obese, and only if diets and exercise have failed to help them shed dangerous fat, British doctors said on Wednesday.
The Royal College of Physicians guidelines on prescription slimming drugs also recommended that the drugs only be prescribed for three months and then assessed for efficacy and safety.
The recommendations underline fears that strong prescription medicines could be misused by slimmers looking for a magic pill to help them take off a few pounds.

"The first strategy to reduce weight is a combination of supervised diet, exercise and changes in behaviour patterns," the college, which groups and advises doctors other than surgeons, said in a statement.
"Patients need to be carefully monitored while they are receiving anti-obesity drugs, with special attention paid to reporting of side-effects and adverse reactions."

Currently the main drug used in Britain is dexfenfluramine, licensed by Interneuron Pharmaceuticals under the brand name of Redux. It increases levels of serotonin, a neurotransmitter or message-carrying chemical linked with mood and appetite.

An older version, fenfluramine, is often prescribed in conjunction with another drug, phentermine, which affects adrenaline and produces a mild "high". In the United States this popular combination -- not recommended by the Food and Drug Administration, however -- is called fen-phen.
Many of the drugs can have serious side-effects, including changes in blood pressure and heart rate.
The College recommended that dexfenfluramine be prescribed for no more than a year. "The drug should be stopped in those patients who have not acheieved a 10 percent weight reduction," it said.

However, doctors agree that the drugs are needed. A third of all Americans are overweight and 25 percent cinically obese -- defined as having a body mass index (BMI -- weight in kg divided by height in metres squared) of above 30.
In Britain nearly 14 percent of men and 17 percent of women are clinically obese.
Being overweight is linked with diabetes, high blood pressure, cancer and heart disease.
"Increasing degrees of overweight and obesity must therefore be considered serious medical issues rather than a perversity of current fashion," the college said.
Experts note that weight loss drugs show a pattern of initial weight loss followed by a re-gain after a few months.
